ety.text: From Middle English juel, jewel, juwel, jeuel, jowel, from Anglo-Norman juel, from Old French jouel, joel, joïel, hence French joyau, of uncertain origin. Perhaps based ultimately on Latin gaudium (“joy”), or on Latin iocus (“joke; jest”), or according to Pihan, from Arabic جَوْهَر (jawhar). Compare Medieval Latin jocale. Displaced native Old English māþm.

senses.d: A precious or semi-precious stone; gem, gemstone.
A valuable object used for personal ornamentation, especially one made of precious metals and stones; a piece of jewellery.
ex: Iachimo: 'Tis plate of rare device, and jewels / Of rich and exquisite form, their values great.
Galveston was the jewel of Texas prior to the hurricane.

Had our prince,—
Jewel of children,—seen this hour, he had pair'd
Well with this lord: there was not full a month
Between their births.

senses.d: A bearing for a pivot in a watch, formed of a crystal or precious stone.
Any of various lycaenid butterflies of the genus Hypochrysops.

ex: The area between her eyebrows wrinkled with the increasing circular motions her two fingers made on her jewel.
As a collector, I prefer jewels to digipaks.

senses.d: To bejewel; to decorate or bedeck with jewels or gems.

grp.label: bearing for a pivot in watch

chain.g: A bud or eye of a plant.

ety.text: Borrowed from Old French joie, alternative form of jouel (source of modern French joyau and Spanish joyel), from Latin jocus.
From Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic الحَاجَة (al-ḥāja, “necessary thing; valuable thing”); or الحِلْيَة (al-ḥilya, “ornament”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese joya, from Old French joie (modern joyau), from Vulgar Latin *jocale, from Latin jocus. Compare Catalan joia and Spanish joya.
Borrowed from Latin gemma (“bud on a plant”).
Backformed from Old French joyaus, plural of joyal, variant of jouel, from Latin iocale.
Borrowed from Breton bizoù, bizou (“ring”), from biz (“finger”).
From Old French joiel, a form of jouel (“jewel”).
Inherited from Middle French pierre, from Old French pierre, from Latin petra.
15th-century borrowing from Catalan robí, from Old French rubin, from Medieval Latin rubīnus, from Latin rubeus (“red”) + -īnus (diminutive).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese rubi, from Catalan robí (“ruby”), from Medieval Latin rubīnus, from Latin rubeus (“red”).
Inherited from Middle English juelrye, from Old French juelerye, equivalent to jewel + -ery.

senses.d: Collectively, personal ornamentation such as rings, necklaces, brooches and bracelets, made of precious metals and sometimes set with gemstones.
ex: The jewellery was very expensive in that shop.
She had more jewellery ornamented about her than any three ladies needed.

senses.d: Any tools, instruments, devices, etc., placed within a drill pipe.
The shop from which a jeweller trades or makes jewellery

it:gioielleria.gl: the art or craft of making jewellery
